prompt: In the neighbor output, what does the Interface ID value 3 identify?
options: The neighboring router's interface used for this relationship.
The local OSPF process number on R1.
The third configured IPv6 prefix in the routing table.
The number of Full neighbors on Gi0/0.
explanation: It is the neighbor's own interface ID for the link. The Neighbor ID column is the remote RID, and the last column is the local interface.

whyWrong.1: The process number is not in this column.
whyWrong.2: It is an interface identifier, not a prefix index.
whyWrong.3: The row is one neighbor, not a count.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R1# show ipv6 ospf neighbor
Neighbor ID     Pri State        Dead Time Interface ID Interface
2.2.2.2          50 FULL/BDR     00:00:35  3            GigabitEthernet0/0

prompt: Which source address does an OSPFv3 Hello use on an ordinary IPv6 Ethernet link?
options: The interface global unicast address.
The interface link-local unicast address.
The multicast address ff02::5.
The 32-bit dotted-decimal router ID.
explanation: OSPFv3 sends packets from the interface's link-local address. Hellos go to the multicast group ff02::5.

whyWrong.0: Neighbors communicate with link-local source addresses.
whyWrong.2: ff02::5 is a destination, not a source.
whyWrong.3: The RID is an identifier, not an IPv6 address.

prompt: A direct two-router adjacency shows FULL/ -. What does the dash mean?
options: The neighbor has no link-local address.
The neighbor has not completed database synchronization.
No DR or BDR role applies to that point-to-point adjacency.
The local process has no router ID.
explanation: The suffix shows the DR/BDR role. A dash appears on point-to-point links because there is no DR or BDR election.

whyWrong.0: A neighbor needs a link-local address to form an adjacency at all.
whyWrong.1: FULL means the databases are synchronized.
whyWrong.3: The adjacency already has a router ID.

prompt: Two routers on an IPv6 Ethernet link have unique RIDs and link-local addresses. Which TWO values must match to become OSPFv3 neighbors?
options: Local process ID
Area ID
Global unicast prefix
Instance ID
Interface priority
explanation: The area ID and instance ID are carried in every OSPFv3 packet and must match. Process IDs, priorities and global prefixes need not.

whyWrong.0: The process ID is local.
whyWrong.2: OSPFv3 uses link-local addresses, so global prefixes need not match.

prompt: What are the default OSPFv3 Hello and dead intervals on broadcast and point-to-point links?
options: 10 seconds and 40 seconds.
3 seconds and 10 seconds.
1 second and approximately 3.6 seconds.
30 seconds and 120 seconds.
explanation: OSPFv3 uses the OSPFv2 defaults: Hello 10 seconds and dead 40 seconds.

whyWrong.2: 1 second and about 3.6 seconds are VRRP timers.
whyWrong.3: 30 and 120 are defaults for non-broadcast network types.

prompt: R2 is IPv6-only and OSPFv3 cannot select a router ID. What is the fix?
options: Use R2 link-local IPv6 address as the router-id value.
Match R2 local process number to R1 so it can inherit R1 identity.
Use R1's existing RID so both routers join the same process.
Configure an explicit unique RID such as 2.2.2.2.
explanation: OSPFv3 still needs a 32-bit router ID, so configure a unique one with router-id.

whyWrong.0: A router ID is 32 bits, not an IPv6 address.
whyWrong.1: The process number does not supply an ID.
whyWrong.2: Router IDs must be unique.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text: %OSPFv3-4-NORTRID: OSPFv3 process 20 could not pick a router-id, please configure manually

prompt: R1 has IPv6 addresses and OSPFv3 process 10 with RID 1.1.1.1. Which TWO commands are still missing?
options: ipv6 unicast-routing in global mode
network 2001:db8:123::/64 area 0 in process mode
ip ospf 10 area 0 in interface mode
ipv6 ospf 10 area 0 in Gi0/0 mode
router-id 2001:db8::1 in process mode
explanation: ipv6 unicast-routing enables IPv6 forwarding, and ipv6 ospf 10 area 0 enables OSPFv3 on the interface.

whyWrong.2: ip ospf activates OSPFv2.
whyWrong.4: A router ID is 32 bits, not an IPv6 address.

prompt: A router has router ospfv3 10 with address-family ipv6 unicast. Which interface command enables it in area 0?
options: ip ospf 10 area 0
ospfv3 10 ipv4 area 0
ospfv3 10 ipv6 area 0
network 2001:db8:123::/64 area 0
explanation: The address-family form is ospfv3 process ipv6 area.

whyWrong.0: This enables OSPFv2.

prompt: Which value is the next hop for packets to the global prefix?
options: Interface ID 7 without any IPv6 address
FE80::13:3 together with local Gi0/1
Local process 10 together with area 0
3.3.3.3 interpreted as the IPv6 next hop
explanation: The next hop is the neighbor's link-local address with the local exit interface. The RID and interface ID are identifiers, not next hops.

whyWrong.0: An interface ID is not an IPv6 address.
whyWrong.2: Process and area are local configuration.
whyWrong.3: A RID is not an IPv6 next hop.

exhibit.title: Neighbor identity and IPv6 route (exercise)
exhibit.text:
R1 process 10, area 0
Neighbor RID 3.3.3.3, Interface ID 7, FULL/ -, local Gi0/1
O 2001:db8:30::/64 [110/26]
  via FE80::13:3, GigabitEthernet0/1

prompt: Which TWO statements about this IPv6-only transit are correct?
options: The missing transit global prefix prevents all global client traffic from crossing.
Routes to the global client prefixes can use scoped link-local next hops.
The global destination must be rewritten to the link-local next hop at every router.
The link-local addresses can support the OSPFv3 adjacency.
Each transit interface must first receive an IPv4 address.
explanation: OSPFv3 neighbors communicate over link-local addresses, and routes to global prefixes can use link-local next hops. The transit needs no IPv4 address.

whyWrong.0: Global traffic can cross links that have only link-local next hops.
whyWrong.2: The packet destination stays the remote global address.
whyWrong.4: A manual 32-bit RID removes the need for an IPv4 address.

exhibit.title: IPv6-only transit requirements (exercise)
exhibit.text:
R1/R2 Ethernet transit has only unique link-local addresses.
Both use explicit unique RIDs, area 0 and matching OSPFv3 settings.
Their separate client LANs have global /64s activated in OSPFv3.
IPv6 forwarding is enabled; no filters.

prompt: R3 Loopback0 is 2001:db8:3::3/64, and R1 learns it as a /128. Why?
options: Normal loopback advertisement represents the interface address as a host route.
OSPFv3 must advertise the configured /64 from every interface state.
The remote router must widen the received /128 to /64 before installation.
A Full adjacency always converts every prefix into a /128.
explanation: OSPFv3 advertises a loopback interface address as a /128 host route.

whyWrong.2: The remote router installs the /128 as advertised.
whyWrong.3: LAN prefixes are still advertised as /64.

prompt: Two routers on one Ethernet link have matching OSPFv3 parameters but global prefixes 2001:db8:1::/64 and 2001:db8:2::/64. What is true?
options: They must fail Hellos because an IPv6 subnet mask field differs.
They can form an adjacency, but that does not validate the intended global addressing.
Their global prefixes must match before either router can advertise any other LAN.
Full adjacency would prove that both configured global prefixes follow the site addressing plan.
explanation: OSPFv3 neighbors use link-local addresses, so they can become adjacent. The adjacency does not check the global addressing plan.

whyWrong.0: OSPFv3 Hellos have no subnet mask field.
whyWrong.2: Global prefixes need not match.
whyWrong.3: A Full adjacency does not verify the addressing plan.

prompt: R1 is a DROTHER and R2 and R3 are the DR and BDR. R1's priority is raised from 1 to 200. What happens?
options: R1 preempts R2 and becomes DR as soon as its next Hello arrives.
R1 keeps its current role while the existing DR/BDR remain healthy.
R1 must become BDR because the new priority is highest.
R1 stops forming adjacencies because 200 is outside the range.
explanation: DR election does not preempt. R1 keeps its role until the DR or BDR fails.

whyWrong.0: A new priority does not take over an existing DR.
whyWrong.2: The existing BDR is not replaced either.

prompt: A fresh election starts with no DR or BDR. Who becomes DR and BDR?
options: RID 4.4.4.4 is DR; RID 3.3.3.3 is BDR.
RID 2.2.2.2 is DR; RID 4.4.4.4 is BDR.
RID 1.1.1.1 is DR; RID 3.3.3.3 is BDR.
The highest global IPv6 address is DR; the next highest is BDR.
explanation: Priority 0 is ineligible. Among the rest, equal priorities are broken by the highest RID.

whyWrong.1: 2.2.2.2 has priority 0, so it is ineligible.
whyWrong.2: Higher RIDs win among equal priorities.
whyWrong.3: The tiebreaker is the router ID, not an address.

prompt: R1 is a DROTHER and shows R4 in 2-Way, with its DR and BDR neighbors Full. What does this mean?
options: The global /64 masks must differ.
Bidirectional Hellos work, and this DROTHER pair need not become Full.
The link-local addresses must be duplicated.
R1 should clear its process until every neighbor becomes Full.
explanation: Two DROTHERs stay at 2-Way. Full adjacencies are only with the DR and BDR.

whyWrong.0: Prefix masks are not involved.
whyWrong.2: The entry does not show duplicate addresses.
whyWrong.3: No reset is needed for a normal 2-Way.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
Neighbor ID  Pri State          Dead Time Interface ID Interface
4.4.4.4       1 2WAY/DROTHER   00:00:34  4            Gi0/0

prompt: R1 reaches R3 directly at outgoing cost 25 or via a shared segment at cost 10. R3's LAN cost is 1. Which route matches the lower-cost path?
options: [110/26] via FE80::13:3, GigabitEthernet0/1
[11/110] via FE80::3, GigabitEthernet0/0
[110/10] via 3.3.3.3, GigabitEthernet0/0
[110/11] via FE80::3, GigabitEthernet0/0
explanation: The shared path costs 10 + 1 = 11. The next hop is R3's link-local address on R1's exit interface.

whyWrong.0: This is the more expensive direct path.
whyWrong.1: The bracket shows distance first, then metric.
whyWrong.2: This leaves out the LAN cost and uses a RID as the next hop.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R1 Gi0/0: shared path, next hop FE80::3, cost 10
R1 Gi0/1: direct path, next hop FE80::13:3, cost 25
R3 LAN: 2001:db8:30::/64, outgoing cost 1

prompt: Which mismatch prevents this OSPFv3 relationship?
options: The router IDs differ.
The global prefixes are absent from the transit interfaces.
The local process numbers differ.
The on-link instance IDs differ.
explanation: OSPFv3 neighbors must have matching area, timers and instance ID. Here the instance IDs differ.

whyWrong.0: Router IDs must be different.
whyWrong.1: Neighbors use link-local addresses, not global prefixes.
whyWrong.2: Process numbers are local.

exhibit.title: Intended neighbor parameters (exercise)
exhibit.text:
R1/R2 directly connected, link-local ping succeeds, no filters.
R1: process 10, RID 1.1.1.1, area 0, instance 0, Hello/dead 10/40
R2: process 20, RID 2.2.2.2, area 0, instance 1, Hello/dead 10/40
Both interfaces activated and non-passive; network type point-to-point.

prompt: What does this dual-stack status show?
options: OSPFv2 Full proves that IPv6 prefixes are also exchanged.
IPv4 OSPF is healthy on this link; IPv6 needs its own OSPFv3 activation and verification.
Giving OSPFv3 the same process number as OSPFv2 automatically activates the interface.
The IPv6 failure proves that the Ethernet cable is down.
explanation: OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 are separate. IPv4 OSPF working says nothing about IPv6; OSPFv3 must be enabled on the interface.

whyWrong.0: OSPFv2 carries only IPv4 routes.
whyWrong.2: A matching process number does not enable the interface.
whyWrong.3: The IPv4 adjacency shows the link is up.

exhibit.title: Separate IPv4 and IPv6 routing state (exercise)
exhibit.text:
R1/R2 IPv4 OSPFv2 neighbors: FULL/ - on Gi0/0
IPv6 link-local ping on Gi0/0 succeeds.
R1 Gi0/0 has no classic ipv6 ospf or address-family ospfv3 activation.
R1 IPv6 OSPF neighbor table is empty.

prompt: Which correction is supported without changing the working transit relationship?
options: Make the transit global prefixes identical before checking the client LAN.
Change R3 router ID to 2001:db8:30::1.
Remove passive status so that the PC can become an OSPFv3 neighbor.
Correct R3 LAN prefix to the approved :30: /64 and verify its advertisement.
explanation: The transit adjacency is Full, but R3 advertises :300: while the plan says :30:. Correct the LAN prefix.

whyWrong.0: The transit adjacency already works.
whyWrong.1: A router ID does not set a LAN prefix.
whyWrong.2: PCs do not form OSPF neighbors.

exhibit.title: Client plan and advertised global prefix (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Approved PC LAN: 2001:db8:30::/64
PC-B: 2001:db8:30::10/64; gateway FE80::30:1
R3 LAN: 2001:db8:300::1/64, FE80::30:1, up, passive, OSPFv3 activated
R1/R3 transit Full; R1 learns 2001:db8:300::/64, not :30: /64.

prompt: R1 and R3 are Full, but R1 lacks R3's LAN prefix 2001:db8:30::/64. Which line is missing?
options: no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/2 under process 30
An IPv4 address on R3's Gi0/2
ipv6 ospf 30 area 0 on R3's Gi0/2
ipv6 ospf priority 255 on R3's Gi0/2
explanation: Gi0/2 has an address but is not enabled in OSPFv3. Add ipv6 ospf 30 area 0 on it.

whyWrong.0: The client LAN should stay passive.
whyWrong.1: An IPv4 address is not needed.
whyWrong.3: Priority does not enable the interface.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R3# show running-config — relevant excerpts
interface GigabitEthernet0/2
 ipv6 address FE80::30:1 link-local
 ipv6 address 2001:DB8:30::1/64
!
ipv6 router ospf 30
 router-id 3.3.3.3
 passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/2

prompt: The transit adjacency is Full but a remote LAN prefix is missing. What is the best next step?
options: Clear both OSPFv3 processes first because any missing route requires a fresh election.
Enable Hellos on the passive client LAN before checking its OSPFv3 activation.
Compare the remote LAN activation and prefix with the route table while preserving the Full transit adjacency.
Replace all link-local addresses because global destinations cannot use them as next hops.
explanation: The transit adjacency is healthy, so check that the remote LAN interface is up and enabled in OSPFv3.

whyWrong.0: A restart does not enable a LAN.
whyWrong.1: A client LAN can stay passive and still be advertised.

exhibit.title: Neighbor and missing LAN evidence (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Remote PC can ping its local router.
R1 and that router are Full on the transit.
R1 lacks the remote client /64 and has no default.
The remote LAN OSPFv3 activation has not yet been checked.

prompt: The direct adjacency stalls in ExStart. What does the comparison show?
options: An area mismatch during Hello acceptance.
A mismatch between local process labels.
An election failure because no DR exists.
An MTU mismatch during database exchange.
explanation: The interface MTUs differ. A mismatch stalls database exchange in ExStart.

whyWrong.0: Both areas are 0.
whyWrong.2: Point-to-point links have no DR election.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R1: Area 0, Instance 0, RID 1.1.1.1, POINT_TO_POINT, Hello 10, Dead 40, MTU 1500
R3: Area 0, Instance 0, RID 3.3.3.3, POINT_TO_POINT, Hello 10, Dead 40, MTU 1400
Neighbor repeatedly EXSTART/ -

prompt: Which route prediction is correct for both routers?
options: Both directions use the direct link at cost 6.
R1: shared path, cost 17. R3: direct path, cost 6.
R1 uses cost 27 shared; R3 uses cost 36 direct.
Both directions use the shared link at cost 17.
explanation: Each router adds its own outgoing costs. R1 compares 17 with 37, and R3 compares 21 with 6.

whyWrong.0: R1's direct path costs 37, not 6.
whyWrong.2: The totals are miscalculated.

exhibit.title: Directed OSPFv3 costs (exercise)
exhibit.text:
All adjacencies Full in area 0; no other paths.
R1 shared outgoing cost 10; direct-to-R3 cost 30.
R3 shared outgoing cost 20; direct-to-R1 cost 5.
LAN-A on R1 cost 1; LAN-B on R3 cost 7.
Use each router own outgoing costs.

prompt: How does OSPFv3 for IPv6 identify itself in the IPv6 header?
options: Next Header 89
UDP port 521
TCP port 179
Next Header 58
explanation: OSPFv3 runs directly over IPv6 with Next Header 89.

whyWrong.1: UDP 521 is not used by OSPFv3.
whyWrong.2: TCP 179 is BGP.

prompt: Which multicast address do OSPFv3 Hellos use?
options: ff02::a
explanation: OSPFv3 Hellos go to ff02::5, all OSPF routers.

whyWrong.1: ff02::6 reaches only the DR and BDR.
whyWrong.2: ff02::1 is all IPv6 nodes.

prompt: What is the default OSPF administrative distance on Cisco IOS?
explanation: OSPF has administrative distance 110.

whyWrong.0: 90 is internal EIGRP.
whyWrong.2: 115 is not used by OSPF.

prompt: What is the default OSPF interface priority?
explanation: The default priority is 1. A priority of 0 makes the interface ineligible for DR and BDR.

whyWrong.0: 0 makes the router ineligible.
whyWrong.2: 100 is not a default.
whyWrong.3: 255 is the highest value, not the default.
